en: Oṃ, homage to the glorious Hevajra!
In the *Jñānapradīpa*, the purification of the symbols of the goddesses has been set forth by me according to their true nature, in due order, and by means of etymological analysis.

Some [perfections] will be explained by way of the nature of the afflictions, some by way of their antidotes, and some by way of the nature of knowledge; furthermore, they will be explained again through their synthesis.

Gaurī holds the maker of the *rohit* (the dawn-red) in her left and right hands; she is so called because she is pure through the concealment of envy (*mātsarya*) from the entire world, and because she is the agent of that [concealment] in the sense of being its cause, or because she consists of the nature of faith and the other [virtues]. Therefore, Gaurī holds the maker of the *rohit* with her left and right hands.

She is *Sūkara* because of the purification of anger (*kopa*) that has arisen easily (*sukara*). In another sādhana, she is called *Koḍa*; even so, the meaning is the same. In the first case, the vowel of the word *sūkara* is lengthened according to etymological rules (*nairukta*). In the second case, there is the substitution of *ḍa* for the *dha* of the word *krodha*. *Ḍamara*s are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and that which is comprised by them; since anger (*krodha*) is among them, she is *Ḍamaru* through the purification that is the pacification of those [afflictions]. Alternatively, she is *Ḍamaru* through the purification that is the departure (*vigama*) of the *ḍamara*s, the afflictions. Therefore, Caurī is the bearer of the *sūkara* and the *ḍamaru*.

"Varāhakṛpīṭadhara" is [stated] elsewhere. Nevertheless, it is consistent; however, there is a difference in terminology and indeed a difference in purification: she is "Varāhakṛpīṭadhara" because she has struck down (āhatavatī) the veil (raṃ). She is "Varāha" because she ascends to the supreme bliss (vara); the meaning is "non-dual mind. "Kṛpīṭa" is the dispelling (sphetaṇa) of the mind that has become miserable (kṛpaṇībhūta). She who holds (dhārayati) those two is Varāhakṛpīṭadhara.

She ascends to bliss (*ānanda*). A *kapāla* is that which protects (*pālayati*) the head (*kaṃ*), that is, happiness; it signifies non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*). Alternatively, it is called a *padma* because one attains (*padyate*), understands, and directly realizes (*sākṣātkriyate*) the ultimate reality within it; thus, it is a vessel (*bhājana*) because it is the support of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-āśrayatvāt*). Because it is free from the stains of cruelty, the *kūrma* is a particular state of mind (*citta-viśeṣa*). Vettālī is so called because she bears both of these—the skull and the tortoise.

Yoga consists of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); that which protects or drinks this is the "yoga-vessel" (*yogapātrī*), which is wisdom (*prajñā*). In another [interpretation], it is called "the oyster shell" (*śukti*). Even so, it remains consistent: it is "the oyster shell" because it dispels sorrow (*śoka*); thus, wisdom itself is the oyster shell. Just as a man possessed of passion (*rāga*) is called a "serpent" (*bhujaṅga*), so too a particular state of mind (*cetoviśeṣa*) possessed of compassionate passion is called a "serpent. In some places, it is read as "all" (*sarve*); because it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is precisely the "middle" state of mind. Because she holds both of these, she is the "Devourer" (*Ghasmarī*) who bears the yoga-vessel and the serpent.

She touches non-abiding nirvāṇa; thus she is the *paraśu* (axe). The *bodhicitta*, inseparable from emptiness and compassion, is the lord (*īśvara*) of what bliss? Who is the lord? The King of Bliss (*sukharāja*). According to etymologists, through the elision of the letter *va*, it becomes *keśara*; that which possesses this is the *keśarī*, a particular state of mind. In some places it is called *siṃha*. And thus, because he destroys all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), he is a *siṃha* (lion), according to the rule beginning with *pṛṣodara*; that too is simply a particular state of mind. She who bears those two [the axe and the lion] is Pukkasī, the bearer of the axe and the lion (*paraśukeśaridharā*).

For instance, due to the application of the sound *khikkhira*, there are the *khikkhirā* and the *paraśukā* and so forth. Likewise, the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*) is the secondary *khikkhirā*. Similarly, for the non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) that is arriving, the conventional sound (*saṅketadhvani*) is the secondary unstruck sound; thus, this too is called *khikkhirā*. That which is begged, requested, or cultivated is the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), namely, non-manifesting gnosis (*nirābhāsajñāna*). She who maintains both of these is the *Khikkhirābhikṣudharā Śavarī*.

Because it ploughs [the field of existence], because it cleaves all adverse factors (*vipakṣa*), right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the "plough" (*lāṅgala*). Because it moves among all sentient beings for the sake of enjoying their virtues, it is the "walking stick" (*caṅkrama*), and so forth; or it is the "knowledge that accomplishes what is to be done" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Or, because it cuts through adverse factors like a wheel, emptiness-knowledge (*śūnyatājñāna*) is the "wheel" (*cakra*). Through the purification of maintaining that [knowledge], the Plough-Wielder and Vajra-Wielder is Caṇḍālī.

Because she makes a threatening gesture that terrifies all the enemies of Māra, she is “Tarjanīkarā” (she whose hand is in the threatening pose). Because of her similarity to a vajra—both in being indestructible by others and in her capacity to cause dissension among others—and because she has the form of that vajra which is like space (*khasama*) and is gnosis (*jñāna*), Dombī is “Vajrakarā” (she whose hand is a vajra).
Thus is the purification of the marks.
Having established the supreme purity of the true signs,
which is the ultimate reality of the hosts of deities;

"By this merit of mine, which has arisen as exceedingly pure, may the Jina [Buddha] be swiftly attained by the world. Thus ends this *Cihnaviśuddhi*. This is the work of the great paṇḍita and master, the venerable Divākaracandra. Om.
